summary: A weekly sales coaching one-to-one in which Chris Klevan reviews a recording of one of Richard Claessen's recent closing calls, pausing throughout to critique. The reviewed prospect is a 52-year-old diabetic dentist with multiple active injuries — forearms, shoulder, rear deltoid and lower right back — who has stopped deadlifting and weighted squatting entirely and reported pain on the clean and press. Chris's core coaching is that Richard talks and coaches too much, asks leading questions, seeks the prospect's approval, and delivers a generic rather than customised pitch. He instructs Richard to stay neutral in discovery, to let the prospect sell himself, and to rebuild the pitch around the prospect's specific injuries and goals. They also discuss an earlier prospect who wanted in-person training and should have been disqualified, and the general problem of prospects ghosting after verbal commitments and deposits. The session is entirely about sales technique; no clinical, pricing or compliance topic is raised by either participant.
notable: The flagship price is confirmed internally at $6,000 by the manager: 'so that way then they're like oh wow yes $6,000? Easy.' This is material context for the separate finding that on 06/30 the same rep described the one-to-one programme to another prospect as 'usually in a couple of thousands'.

Chris states that $1,000 deposits are an established practice he has personally taken: 'I've had people that put down $1,000 deposits and told me for sure next week, they're going to come in and they're going to get this credit card and they ghost me even with the $1,000 deposit.' Richard, by contrast, improvised $100 and $200 deposits on both of his 06/29 calls and presented $200 as the customary figure. No standard deposit amount or refund policy is stated anywhere in the session.
Richard describes a prospect as 'a little bit zesty', Chris asks 'Oh, you mean gay?', and Richard confirms. The manager does not correct the characterisation and the conversation moves on.

Richard admits knowingly pitching a prospect he had already assessed as a poor fit: 'I pitched for the sake of pitching.' Chris agrees the correct move was to disqualify — 'dude, it sounds like you want a personal trainer, and honestly, that's just not what we do' — which is a clear statement that disqualification is expected practice.

Chris coaches Richard to withhold a favourable assessment of a prospect's diet, explicitly because it undermines the nutrition pillar: 'because of earlier you told him his diet is good, the nutrition part is going to be tough for you to land now' and 'you want to withhold comments about if their diet being good or anything like that. You want to stay neutral.'

The reviewed prospect challenged the programme's therapeutic claims directly — 'it's quite a big claim. I've noticed that you're saying kettlebells will eliminate... these small pains' — and neither participant discussed whether the claim is substantiated. The coaching response was about how Richard should have reframed the word 'skeptical' to make the prospect sell himself.

Richard names his own recurring pattern as people-pleasing and seeking prospect approval; Chris coaches him to accept the emotion rather than suppress it. Richard's stated takeaways are to stop coaching mid-call and to make the pitch feel custom.
Chris articulates the value model plainly: 'That's why somebody would pay $6,000 is to transform into that. They have to believe that it's possible and that this program can do it for them.'

Two named prospects are discussed as pending deals — a 'Jacob guy' working through a credit union on payments who has stopped responding, and a 'Tyler guy' who did not follow through. Richard says of Jacob 'I want to do it with the 20', which is not explained.
Richard mentions he will present projections at a team meeting the following day.
